ai_summary: Scotland’s electricity system continues to highlight a stark operational divergence within the national energy network, recording a Scottish carbon intensity of 0 gCO2/kWh versus 102 gCO2/kWh GB-wide. Across the broader network, GB wind output has reached 9.7 GW, with estimated Scottish wind output contributing 3.9 GW, representing 38.6% of installed Scottish wind capacity. However, persistent structural bottlenecks along cross-border transmission corridors prevent the full absorption of this clean generation into high-demand areas. As a direct consequence, Scottish generation curtailed so far today sits at 5456.4 MWh, accumulating an avoidable constraint cost of about £141,634. Beyond the direct financial burden placed on system balancing, this enforced renewable curtailment drives significant carbon leakage. Fossil-fueled generation must be dispatched to plug the localized deficit, leading to an estimated 1036716.0 m3 of gas burned elsewhere to replace it and generating 1909.7 tonnes CO2. These figures clearly demonstrate that without accelerated transmission infrastructure investment, abundant Scottish wind generation will remain stranded behind grid constraints, escalating balancing expenses while driving avoidable reliance on fossil thermal assets elsewhere across Great Britain.
